query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings applied on conventional metal substrates, a controlled pre-oxidation treatment forms a coherent duplex oxide scale that, in tandem with thermally activated grain-boundary diffusion (including possible Cu segregation), stabilizes the microstructure. This combined effect provides both a solid-lubricant interphase and a load-bearing barrier that reduces both adhesive and abrasive wear at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment by holding the as-deposited coating at a defined temperature (e.g., 350–400°C) under a controlled oxygen partial pressure for a set duration to tailor the formation of a duplex oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted in the temperature range of 300°C to 600°C under moderate to high sliding/contact loads representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A duplex oxide scale formed on the coating surface, together with a stabilized nano-structured microstructure achieved by thermally activated grain boundary diffusion and Cu segregation.
generation.mechanism: The controlled oxidation induces the formation of a protective duplex oxide layer which acts both as a solid lubricant and as an effective load-bearing interphase during wear. Concurrently, elevated temperatures activate grain-boundary diffusion (with potential Cu segregation) that helps stabilize the microstructure against coarsening, collectively delaying or reducing both adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Wear tests under the defined conditions will show a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rates for the pre-oxidized coatings compared to the unmodified, as-deposited baseline. Microstructural analysis should reveal a coherent, stable duplex oxide on the surface and evidence of limited grain coarsening.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 300°C to 600°C; Loading: moderate to high sliding/contact loads that simulate high-temperature, protective coating service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of the duplex oxide scale versus the thermally activated grain-boundary diffusion (and Cu segregation effects) in reducing wear are not fully quantified, and the optimum pre-oxidation parameters (temperature, duration, oxygen pressure) remain to be precisely defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples: one set as-deposited, and one set pre-treated with a controlled pre-oxidation process. Subject both sets to high-temperature wear testing in the 300–600°C range under identical moderate-to-high contact loads. Perform surface and cross-sectional characterization (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to evaluate oxide layer coherence, thickness, and microstructural stability.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Microstructural analysis of the oxide layer and underlying coating
Grain size and evidence of Cu segregation at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a coherent, duplex oxide layer, or if they fail to demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the as-deposited baseline (or even show degraded performance), then the hypothesis is falsified.

They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. frame.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings is governed by a synergistic mechanism wherein controlled oxidation induces the formation of a stable, duplex oxide scale that acts both as a solid lubricant and as a load-bearing interphase, while thermally activated grain boundary diffusion (possibly aided by Cu segregation) stabilizes the microstructure. This combined effect delays abrasive and adhesive wear. An intervention would be to apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to the baseline as-deposited coating to tailor the oxide scale formation. If the hypothesis is correct, wear tests conducted between 300°C and 600°C under defined loading conditions should show a reduced friction coefficient and lower wear rates for the pre-oxidized coatings compared to unmodified ones. Conversely, failure to observe the formation of a coherent oxide layer or detection of rapid oxide spallation and degradation of the coating upon high-temperature sliding would falsify the hypothesis. This mechanism connects to prior evidence on the beneficial role of protective oxides and diffusion-induced microstructural stabilization in similar high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys.

decision.trend: Earlier work on high-entropy alloy coatings largely focused on room‐temperature wear behavior with variations in composition, grain size, and substrate adhesion. More recent studies on related systems have extended the temperature range, revealing that at elevated temperatures (e.g., 500–900°C) the formation of protective oxide phases (such as spinels) can significantly reduce wear. Additionally, work on sputtered or nanocrystalline films has begun to show that annealing and thermal treatments modify the microstructure—inducing controlled oxidation and affecting grain boundary diffusion—which in turn influences wear resistance. However, these studies have either examined the oxide formation in isolation or considered bulk alloy responses rather than addressing the integrated behavior of a thin protective coating across a broad high‐temperature regime.
decision.unsolved: For FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings under high-temperature wear, the combined mechanistic roles of controlled oxidation (yielding a duplex oxide layer acting as both a solid lubricant and load‐bearing interphase) and thermally activated grain boundary diffusion (with possible Cu segregation stabilizing the microstructure) have not been directly tested. It remains unclear how a pre-formed, stable oxide layer interacts with the evolving microstructure under sliding loads at 300–600°C, and what treatment conditions optimize this synergy.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (adjusting parameters such as treatment temperature, duration, and oxygen partial pressure) on the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating
decision.why: Because recent evidence from similar HEA coatings indicates that preformed oxide scales can improve wear performance at high temperatures by serving dual roles in lubrication and load bearing, and controlling the grain-boundary diffusion (including Cu segregation). Systematically varying the pre-oxidation parameters will test whether forming a coherent, duplex oxide scale can synergistically interact with the microstructure to delay both adhesive and abrasive wear, consistent with the emerging trend of leveraging controlled oxidation for enhanced high-temperature tribological behavior.
